text: Screen shot-based computer use takes three to eight seconds every single time the agent looks at the screen. Virsel's new agent desktop reads the real UI in 50 to 200 milliseconds, because it never takes a screenshot at all. It asks the operating system for the actual structure of every window, free and open source, on Mac, Windows, and Linux. There is one place this approach genuinely breaks down though, and that part of the story is coming before the end. This comes from Virsel Labs, the experimental arm of the company behind Next.js, with nearly 10,000 followers and 395 public repositories on GitHub. Chris Tate announced it on October 31st with one line, "Agent browser for your whole computer." That framing matters, because Agent Browser already won a following as the token efficient way for agents to drive websites. Agent Desktop extends the same philosophy past the browser to every app on your machine. On Prism Labs, computer use infrastructure is exactly the layer we watch. Here's the core idea, straight from the docs. Instead of looking at pixels, Agent Desktop asks the OS Accessibility API, the same layer screen readers use, for the live structure of an app. A snapshot returns Jason with a ref for every element an agent can act on. Every button, every text field, labeled by role. The agent clicks or types against a ref, then snapshots again to verify what changed, observe, act, observe. Ref stays stable across snapshots, actions are safe to retry, and nothing is inferred from a picture. If you've ever watched a vision agent click two pixels left of a button, you already know why this matters. The performance difference isn't subtle. Third party testing puts an accessibility tree read at 50 to 200 milliseconds, a typical snapshot lands around 120. Screen shot vision computer use, the approach used by the big model driven loops, needs three to eight seconds per observation. Because a frontier model has to look at an image and reason about coordinates every step. Through the native binary, a single agent desktop call runs in about 21 milliseconds. When an agent needs 50 observations to finish a task, that's the difference between seconds and minutes. And because snapshots are plain Jason, you're not paying vision token prices for every glance either. It installs as one NPM package, snapshot an app and you get the interactive elements with their refs. Act on a ref, click it, type into it, set a value, and the tool confirms delivery before returning. Notice the ref format, the snapshot ID and element ID travel together. So a stale ref from an old snapshot gets rejected instead of silently clicking the wrong thing. That one design decision kills the classic computer use failure mode, where the screen changed and the agent didn't notice. This is the entire contract between the agent and your desktop. Structured Jason, a snapshot ID and a list of elements with role, label, and value. No bounding boxes to estimate, no OCR, no coordinates. A language model can read this directly in a few hundred tokens. Compare that to shipping a full screen shot into a vision model on every step. It's the same trick that made agent browser popular on the web, applied to native apps. Give the model text, because text is what models are actually good at. The safety model is unusually conservative and honestly refreshing. Headless by default, it never moves your pointer or steals focus unless you explicitly pass the headed flag. Raw, key down and mouse down primitives, flat out refuse to run until the team trusts their release mechanics. Protected OS processes can't be closed. On Windows, elevated apps reject standard collars with a permission error instead of letting an agent escalate. The pattern across all of it, when in doubt, refuse. Make the agent's world predictable rather than powerful. The numbers moved fast for infrastructure this low level. 8,778 stars and 609 forks within days of the version 1.0 announcement. More than 60 commands across all three platforms, and it isn't locked to any one agent. It ships as a plain CLI, as an installable skill through the skills ecosystem, and as a C library for in-process calls, with Python bindings demonstrated in the docs. Clawed code, codex, cursor, or your own script. Anything that can run a shell command can drive a desktop with it. That neutrality is rare. Most computer use stacks assume you've married one vendor's agent. Put it next to the incumbent approach in the architectural split is clean. Anthropic, open AI, and Gemini computer use all work the same way. Screen shot, sent to model, infer coordinates, click, repeat. The model is in the loop for every observation. Agent desktop has no model inside at all. It's deterministic tooling the model calls, like a compiler or a database client. Screen shot loops handle anything visible, including canvas. Tree reads handle anything labeled instantly and cheaply. That trade is the whole debate, and it's where the criticism lands. Developer Flavio copes ran an end-to-end on Linux and summed up the design in one line. The agent observes, acts, and observes again. There is no pixel match in that loop. His testing confirmed the claimed behavior. Real text landed in a real editor, edits came back verified, and the auto-weight handled timing without sleeps. For a tool four days past its 1.0, independent reproduction matters more than any benchmark slide. The repository is pure rust with platform adapters per OS. The accessibility API on Mac OS, UI Automation on Windows, ATSPI on Linux, releases moved quickly, version 1.0.0 on October 28, a patch the same night, 1.0.2 two days later, with the public announcement following on the 31st. There's one more clever bridge in here, for electron and chromium apps, where accessibility labels get thin. Agent desktop can open a DevTools port, and hand the web content over to Agent Browser. The two tools are designed to meet in the middle. And here's the catch I promised at the top. The community reaction is split along one line. Accessibility trees are only as good as the labels developers bother to write. Canvas rendered apps are invisible to this approach. Electron apps with half-missing labels give you half a UI. The counterpoint that DevTools hand off to Agent Browser covers exactly the worst offenders. And for everything else, screenshot fallback still exists. Others are simply relieved someone is unifying computer use across Claude, chat GPT, and GROC, instead of shipping another silo. The timeline shows patience, then a sprint. The repo started quietly in February 2026. Through Spring and Summer, it iterated on the REF model and the per-platform adapters. Version 1.0.0 landed October 28, got patched within hours, and 1.0.2 followed on the 30th. Then the announcement on Halloween, after the stable release, not before it. Versel shipped the software first and the hype second, which tells you who they built it for. For a category this failure prone, that ordering is the credibility signal. Agent desktop is free, a patchy 2.0, and linked below next to Agent hyphen browser. Subscribe to Prism Labs. Agent Infrastructure moves weekly, and we keep you a step ahead of all of it.
